blocks.text: Psalms arose within Israel’s worship and could be sung in both public and private devotion. Although poetic prayer was common in the ancient world, the Psalms characteristically bind human emotion to covenant faith. Psalm 22 therefore speaks both as an intensely personal cry and as words suited to the assembly that joins its praise.

sections.title: A Psalm as Prayer and Song

blocks.text: Psalm 22 begins with protest over God’s apparent absence, continues through petition and remembered trust, and ends in public praise. One influential interpretation sees this range as characteristic of the Psalter: faithful speech to YHWH is not limited to praise but can include lament, protest, confession, petition, trust, and thanksgiving. On this reading, the psalm’s opening anguish and closing praise belong to one sustained act of addressing God.

Psalm 22:1 also figures in interpretations of Mark’s crucifixion account. Mark presents a Roman public execution surrounded by royal mockery, abandonment, scriptural lament, darkness, death, a torn curtain, contested recognition, and women’s witness. Reading the cry of abandonment within that larger narrative connects it with a scene of public shame and suffering, though interpreters dispute how all these elements should be understood together.
